name: Interview statistics, set 1
description: Statistics questions of the kind asked in online assessments and first rounds: estimators, intervals, p-values, power, regression slopes, time-series moments and correlation limits. Each item keeps its own schedule.

items.prose: You time six gaps between your own fills, in seconds: 4, 9, 2, 7, 5 and 3. You model each gap as exponential with rate $\lambda$ per second.
items.question: What is the maximum-likelihood estimate of $\lambda$, as a decimal?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write the log-likelihood in $\lambda$ and set its derivative to zero.

byKey.mean-wait: You gave the mean wait of 5 seconds. The rate is its reciprocal, 1/5 a second.
byKey.five-gaps: You divided 5 by the total. Six gaps were timed, so the count on top is 6.

explain.text: The log-likelihood is $6\ln\lambda - 30\lambda$. Its derivative $6/\lambda - 30$ is zero at $\lambda = 6/30 = 0.2$. The estimate is the number of gaps over their total time.

items.prose: A share closes at 4, 7, 9 and 12 on four days.
items.question: What is the unbiased sample variance of the four closes, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Sum the squared deviations from the mean, then divide by one less than the count.

byKey.divide-by-n: You divided by 4. The unbiased estimate divides by n - 1 = 3, because the mean was fitted from the same data.
byKey.gave-sd: You took the square root. The question asks for the variance, 34/3, not the standard deviation.

explain.text: The mean is 8, so the deviations are -4, -1, 1 and 4, whose squares sum to 34. Dividing by $n - 1 = 3$ corrects for measuring them from the sample mean. That gives $34/3 \approx 11.33$.

items.prose: A 95% confidence interval for a mean, built from 64 observations, has half-width 2.94.
items.question: How many observations give a half-width of 1.47, if the spread of the data stays the same?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the half-width depends on n.

byKey.doubled-n: You doubled n. The half-width falls with the square root of n, so halving it needs four times the data.
byKey.halved-n: You halved n, which widens the interval. A narrower interval needs more data, not less.

explain.text: The half-width is $1.96\,s/\sqrt{n}$, so it shrinks with $\sqrt{n}$. Halving it needs $\sqrt{n}$ twice as large, so n four times as large. That is $4 \times 64 = 256$.

items.prose: Your prior for a courier's on-time rate is Beta(3, 1). Then 7 of 10 parcels arrive on time.
items.question: What is the posterior mean? Give 4 decimal places or a fraction.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the prior counts to the observed counts first.

byKey.no-prior: You used 7/10 and left the prior out. Beta(3, 1) adds 3 on time and 1 late.
byKey.one-each: You added one of each. This prior adds 3 on time and 1 late.

explain.text: A Beta(3, 1) prior acts like 3 parcels on time and 1 late seen before. The posterior is Beta(10, 4). Its mean is $10/14 \approx 0.7143$.

items.prose: You flip a coin 16 times and see 13 heads.
items.question: What is the exact two-sided p-value against a fair coin, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Add the binomial chances of 13 or more heads, then allow for the other tail.

byKey.one-tail: You kept one tail only. A two-sided test also counts 3 or fewer heads, which is as extreme.
byKey.normal-curve: You used the normal curve at z = 2.5. With 16 flips the exact binomial sum is wanted, and it is larger.

explain.text: Under a fair coin, $P(X \ge 13) = (560 + 120 + 16 + 1)/65536 = 697/65536$. The low tail of 3 or fewer heads has the same chance. The two-sided p-value is $697/32768 \approx 0.0213$.

items.prose: Observations have known standard deviation 12. You take 36 of them and test a mean of 0 against a higher mean, one-sided at 5%. You reject when z exceeds 1.645. In fact the true mean is 4. You are told $\Phi(0.355) = 0.6387$.
items.question: What is the power of the test, to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the sample mean at which you reject, then ask how often a true mean of 4 clears it.

byKey.miss-rate: You gave the chance of missing the shift. Power is one minus that, the chance of rejecting.
byKey.two-sided: You used the two-sided critical value 1.96. This test is one-sided, so the line sits at 1.645.

explain.text: The standard error is $12/6 = 2$, so you reject when the sample mean exceeds $1.645 \times 2 = 3.29$. A true mean of 4 sits $0.71/2 = 0.355$ standard errors above that line. The power is $\Phi(0.355) \approx 0.6387$.

items.prose: You screen a list of candidate signals. The best one has z = 3.2, a two-sided p-value of 0.001374. You will apply a Bonferroni correction at 5% overall.
items.question: What is the largest number of signals the list can hold for this one still to pass?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bonferroni tests each of m signals at 0.05/m; solve for the largest m.

byKey.rounded-up: You rounded 36.39 up. With 37 signals the threshold 0.05/37 falls below 0.001374, so the signal fails.
byKey.one-sided: You halved the p-value to a one-sided one. The question gives the two-sided p-value, and that is the one to test.

explain.text: Bonferroni tests each of m signals at $0.05/m$. The signal passes while $0.001374 \le 0.05/m$, that is while $m \le 36.39$. So the list may hold at most 36 signals.

items.prose: You regress y on x by least squares and get slope 2.5. Regressing x on y gives slope 0.1.
items.question: What is the correlation of x and y, as a decimal?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Write each slope as the correlation times a ratio of standard deviations.

byKey.no-root: You stopped at the product of the slopes. That product is the squared correlation, so take its root.
byKey.ratio: You divided one slope by the other. Multiplying them cancels the standard deviations; dividing does not.

explain.text: The two slopes are $r\,s_y/s_x$ and $r\,s_x/s_y$. Their product is $r^2 = 2.5 \times 0.1 = 0.25$. Both slopes are positive, so $r = 0.5$.

items.prose: A regression of y on one predictor uses 27 points and has $R^2 = 0.2$. The slope is positive.
items.question: What is the t statistic of the slope, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. With one predictor, the squared t statistic is the regression F statistic.

byKey.no-one-minus: You left out the divide by $1 - R^2$. The unexplained share 0.8 sits under the line.
byKey.used-n: You multiplied by n = 27. The residual degrees of freedom are $n - 2 = 25$.
byKey.no-root: You gave $t^2$. Take the square root of 6.25 to get t.

explain.text: With one predictor, $t^2 = R^2 (n - 2)/(1 - R^2)$, which is the F statistic. Here $t^2 = 0.2 \times 25 / 0.8 = 6.25$. So $t = 2.50$.

items.prose: The true model is $y = 1.5x_1 - 2x_2 + \varepsilon$. Regressing $x_2$ on $x_1$ gives slope 0.4.
items.question: You regress y on $x_1$ alone. What slope do you expect, to 1 decimal place?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The left-out variable's effect reaches y through its link with $x_1$.

byKey.no-bias: You kept the true coefficient. Leaving out $x_2$ moves part of its effect onto $x_1$.
byKey.added-bias: You added 2 times 0.4. The coefficient on $x_2$ is -2, so the bias is -0.8.

explain.text: Leaving out $x_2$ moves its effect onto $x_1$ through their link. The slope becomes $1.5 + (-2)(0.4)$. That is $1.5 - 0.8 = 0.7$.

items.prose: A series follows $x_t = 0.6x_{t-1} + e_t$, where $e_t$ is white noise with variance 16.
items.question: What is the stationary variance of $x_t$?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Take the variance of both sides of the equation.

byKey.unsquared: You divided by 1 - 0.6. The coefficient multiplies a variance, so it enters squared: 1 - 0.36.
byKey.noise-only: You gave the noise variance. Yesterday's value carries variance forward too.

explain.text: Take variances of both sides: $V = 0.36V + 16$. So $V = 16/0.64 = 25$. The coefficient enters squared because it scales a variance.

items.prose: A series follows $x_t = e_t + 0.75e_{t-1}$, where $e_t$ is white noise.
items.question: What is the lag-1 autocorrelation of $x_t$, to 2 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Divide the lag-1 covariance by the variance.

byKey.coefficient: You gave the coefficient itself. It must be divided by the variance of $x_t$, which is more than one noise variance.
byKey.unsquared: You divided by 1.75. The variance is $1 + 0.75^2 = 1.5625$ noise variances, with the coefficient squared.

explain.text: The lag-1 covariance is $0.75\sigma^2$, since only $e_{t-1}$ is shared. The variance is $(1 + 0.75^2)\sigma^2 = 1.5625\sigma^2$. Their ratio is $0.75/1.5625 = 0.48$.

items.prose: A strategy's true Sharpe ratio is 1.1 a year. You will judge it by the t statistic of its mean return.
items.question: How long a record gives that t statistic an expected value of 3? Answer in years to 1 decimal place.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Ask how the t statistic of a mean grows with the length of the sample.

byKey.no-square: You stopped at 3/1.1. The t statistic grows with the square root of the years, so square that ratio.
byKey.aimed-at-two: You aimed for a t statistic of 2. The question asks for 3.

explain.text: The t statistic of the mean return is the annual Sharpe ratio times $\sqrt{T}$. Setting $1.1\sqrt{T} = 3$ gives $T = (3/1.1)^2 \approx 7.44$. So you need about 7.4 years.

items.prose: Three variables have corr(X, Y) = 0.28 and corr(Y, Z) = 0.96.
items.question: What is the highest possible corr(X, Z), to 4 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The correlation matrix must have a determinant of at least zero.

byKey.product-only: You multiplied the two correlations. That is the centre of the range; add the root term for the top.
byKey.no-limit: You assumed any value is possible. Strong links through Y pin corr(X, Z) to a range.

explain.text: A correlation matrix must be positive semidefinite, which caps corr(X, Z) at $0.28 \times 0.96 + \sqrt{(1 - 0.28^2)(1 - 0.96^2)}$. The root term is $0.96 \times 0.28$, since $\sqrt{1 - 0.28^2} = 0.96$. So the cap is $0.2688 + 0.2688 = 0.5376$, and the floor is 0.

items.prose: You draw 100 values from a normal distribution with standard deviation 2 and take their median.
items.question: What is the large-sample standard error of the sample median, to 3 decimal places?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The median's standard error depends on the density at the median.

byKey.mean-se: You gave the standard error of the mean, $2/\sqrt{100}$. The median is noisier, by a factor of $\sqrt{\pi/2}$.
byKey.no-root: You multiplied by $\pi/2$. The factor on the variance is $\pi/2$, so the standard error takes its root.

explain.text: For large n the median's standard error is $1/(2f(m)\sqrt{n})$, where $f(m)$ is the density at the median. A normal density at its centre is $1/(\sigma\sqrt{2\pi})$, which turns this into $\sigma\sqrt{\pi/2}/\sqrt{n}$. Here that is $0.2\sqrt{\pi/2} \approx 0.251$.
